WITH inaccurate AS (                         -- one row per inaccurate order, however many reports
  SELECT DISTINCT r.order_id
  FROM issue_reports r
  JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = r.order_id
  WHERE r.issue_type IN ('missing_item', 'incorrect_item')
    AND r.reported_at <= o.delivered_at + INTERVAL '{{window_h}} hours'
)
SELECT s.merchant_id,
       date_trunc('week', o.placed_at AT TIME ZONE {{week_tz_sql}})::date AS week_start,
       o.channel,
       COUNT(*)                                                     AS delivered_orders,
       COUNT(i.order_id)                                            AS inaccurate_orders,
       ROUND((COUNT(*) - COUNT(i.order_id))::numeric / COUNT(*), 4) AS accuracy_rate
FROM orders o
JOIN stores s ON s.store_id = o.store_id
LEFT JOIN inaccurate i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
GROUP BY s.merchant_id, week_start, o.channel
ORDER BY s.merchant_id, week_start, o.channel;

Explanation. The inaccurate set is built once, with DISTINCT, so an order with three reports is one row. Only the two accuracy issue types count, and only inside the inclusive window after delivery; a cancelled order has a NULL delivered_at, so its reports fail the window test, and it is filtered out of the outer query anyway. The LEFT JOIN keeps every delivered order in the denominator and COUNT(i.order_id) counts only those that matched. AT TIME ZONE turns the instant into local wall-clock time before date_trunc('week', …), which starts weeks on Monday. Stores are rolled up to the merchant through stores, and the channel stays in the grouping so the merchant's own channel is a separate row.

Complexity. One pass over reports (a hash join to orders), one hash join and one hash aggregate over orders: O(n) with hashing. At scale, partition orders by week and keep the inaccurate set per week, since reports arrive within the window.

Snowflake: DATE_TRUNC('week', CONVERT_TIMEZONE(time_zone, placed_at)) depends on the WEEK_START parameter, so say which; DATEADD(hour, …). Spark SQL: date_trunc('week', from_utc_timestamp(placed_at, time_zone)) (Monday weeks). MySQL 8: no date_trunc; use DATE_SUB(d, INTERVAL WEEKDAY(d) DAY) on CONVERT_TZ(...), which needs the time zone tables loaded.

Every level: an order with three qualifying reports; a cancelled order with a missing_item report; a delivered order with only a non-accuracy report; an own-channel order with a report; delivered orders with no report. Very Hard: stores in several zones, an order early on Monday UTC that is Sunday evening in the Americas (previous week), and an order late on Sunday UTC that is Monday in Sydney (next week).

Counting reports instead of orders; an inner join to reports, which loses every order without a report and makes accuracy 0; counting cancelled orders in the denominator; counting late-delivery or packaging reports; a strict < at the window; grouping by store instead of merchant; dropping the channel; integer division; weeks in UTC at Very Hard; EXTRACT(WEEK …) without the year.

WITH waived AS (                              -- waived orders per member-month
  SELECT o.consumer_id,
         m.month,
         COUNT(*)                  AS n_orders,
         SUM(o.delivery_fee_cents) AS cents
  FROM orders o
  JOIN stores s ON s.store_id = o.store_id
  JOIN member_months m
    ON m.consumer_id = o.consumer_id
   AND m.month = date_trunc('month', o.placed_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date
  WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
    AND o.subtotal_cents - o.promo_cents >=
        CASE WHEN s.vertical = 'restaurant' THEN {{min_restaurant}} ELSE {{min_grocery}} END
  GROUP BY o.consumer_id, m.month
), per_member AS (
  SELECT m.month,
         CASE WHEN m.is_trial THEN 'trial' ELSE 'paid' END AS plan_kind,
         m.price_cents,
         COALESCE(w.n_orders, 0) AS n_orders,
         COALESCE(w.cents, 0)    AS cents
  FROM member_months m
  LEFT JOIN waived w ON w.consumer_id = m.consumer_id AND w.month = m.month
)
SELECT month, plan_kind,
       COUNT(*)                                   AS members,
       SUM(n_orders)                              AS waived_orders,
       SUM(cents)                                 AS fees_waived_cents,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE cents > price_cents) AS members_ahead,
       ROUND(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE cents > price_cents)::numeric / COUNT(*), 4) AS share_ahead
FROM per_member
GROUP BY month, plan_kind
ORDER BY month, plan_kind;

Explanation. The inner join to member_months on the order's UTC month keeps only orders placed while the consumer was a member; delivered status and the minimum (after promotions, per vertical) decide which fees were waived. Summing per member-month first is essential, because "ahead" compares a member's monthly total with that member's price. The LEFT JOIN back onto member_months keeps members with no waived order (COALESCE to 0), so the share's denominator is every member-month. plan_kind keeps trial months apart.

Complexity. Hash joins and two hash aggregates: O(n) in orders plus member-months. In production, member-months come from billing periods and the waived amount should come from the order's own fee record rather than be recomputed from a rule.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). BigQuery: DATE_TRUNC(DATE(placed_at), MONTH), COUNTIF(cents > price_cents), IF(is_trial, 'trial', 'paid'). Snowflake: DATE_TRUNC('month', placed_at)::date, COUNT_IF, IFF. Spark SQL: trunc(placed_at, 'MM'), count_if. MySQL 8: DATE_FORMAT(placed_at, '%Y-%m-01'), SUM(cents > price_cents).

Edge cases built into the data. Every level: member-months with no orders; a member-month whose waived fees equal the price exactly (not ahead), alongside a cancelled qualifying order and an order a cent below the minimum in that month; non-member months with orders; trial months. Hard: promotions on some orders, an order exactly at the minimum after its promotion (qualifies) and one a cent below after its promotion (does not); orders a second either side of a month boundary for a member who joined in the later month. Very Hard: grocery and convenience stores with a higher minimum, an order between the two minimums at a grocery store (not waived) and one exactly at the grocery minimum (waived).

Common mistakes. An inner join that drops members who saved nothing; >= for "ahead"; summing across all members before comparing with a price; testing the minimum before promotions; one minimum for every vertical; counting cancelled orders; counting non-member orders by joining on consumer only; integer division.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Spread an annual price over its months (state the rule), or compare annual waived fees with the annual price per member; a cancelled annual member needs the refund rule, so say which. (2) Compare cohorts that joined before and after the change, or the same members before and after; a rule change and a mix change move the share together. (3) The waiver is revenue forgone only on orders that would have happened anyway; members order more, so the true cost needs a comparison group. WITH lines AS (                               -- each order line with the item's state at order time
  SELECT o.order_id, o.store_id, o.placed_at,
         (SELECT t.is_available
          FROM availability_toggles t
          WHERE t.item_id = i.item_id
            AND t.toggled_at <= o.placed_at
            AND (t.store_id = o.store_id
                 OR (t.store_id IS NULL AND t.merchant_id = s.merchant_id))
          ORDER BY t.toggled_at DESC, t.toggle_id DESC
          LIMIT 1) AS is_available
  FROM orders o
  JOIN stores s      ON s.store_id = o.store_id
  JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
), per_order AS (
  SELECT order_id, store_id, (placed_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date AS order_date,
         COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE is_available = false) AS bad_lines
  FROM lines
  GROUP BY order_id, store_id, (placed_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date
)
SELECT store_id, order_date,
       COUNT(*)                               AS orders,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE bad_lines > 0)  AS flagged_orders,
       SUM(bad_lines)                         AS flagged_lines
FROM per_order
GROUP BY store_id, order_date
ORDER BY store_id, order_date;

Explanation. The correlated subquery is the as-of lookup: among the toggles for this item that apply to this store (its own, or its merchant's merchant-wide ones at Very Hard) and are at or before the order, take the latest, with toggle_id deciding ties. No row means NULL, and is_available = false is not true for NULL, so an item never toggled is available. Aggregating to one row per order before the store-day keeps orders and lines apart. Below Very Hard no toggle has a NULL store_id, so the merchant-wide branch never fires and the same query serves every level.

Complexity. One index probe per order line with an index on (item_id, toggled_at) (or (store_id, item_id, toggled_at)): O(L log T). Without an index, O(L·T). In a warehouse, an as-of join is a sort-merge: union lines and toggles, sort by (store, item, time, kind) and carry the last state forward with a window function.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). Snowflake: ASOF JOIN … MATCH_CONDITION (o.placed_at >= t.toggled_at) handles one scope; ties need care, and merchant-wide toggles need a second as-of join and a comparison. DuckDB also has ASOF JOIN. BigQuery: no as-of join; use the union-and-LAST_VALUE(… IGNORE NULLS) pattern, or QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() over a join on item and time (expensive). Spark SQL: the union-and-window pattern; a range join hint can help. MySQL 8: a LATERAL derived table with ORDER BY … LIMIT 1.

Edge cases built into the data. Every level: an order before an "off" toggle and one after it; an "off" toggle after every order (ignored); off then back on before an order (available); an order with two unavailable lines; items never toggled. Hard: a toggle at exactly the order time (applies); two toggles at one instant, the higher toggle_id saying available; the same item off at another store only. Very Hard: merchant-wide off then a later store-level on (available); store-level off then a later merchant-wide on (available); a merchant-wide off applying to a second store of the merchant; another merchant's merchant-wide toggle (ignored).

Common mistakes. EXISTS an earlier off toggle (ignores switching back on); MAX(toggled_at) and then a join that returns two rows at a tie; < instead of <=; tie-breaking by the lower id; using toggles from other stores; ignoring merchant-wide toggles, or letting a merchant-wide toggle always beat a store toggle regardless of time; counting lines as orders; dropping store-days with no flagged order.

(2) Partition both sides by store (or item) and date, and use the sort-merge pattern so the join is local; carry the state forward across date boundaries with a daily snapshot of the latest state. (3) Keep the off toggle's time in the as-of lookup and subtract; an item off since before the data starts needs a snapshot or "at least N minutes". from bisect import bisect_right

WEEK = 7 * 1440


def open_store_counts(hours, orders):
    starts, ends = [], []
    for _store, day, open_min, close_min in hours:
        s = day * 1440 + open_min
        e = day * 1440 + close_min if close_min > open_min else (day + 1) * 1440 + close_min
        if e > WEEK:                       # Sunday night into Monday: split at the week's end
            starts += (s, 0)
            ends += (WEEK, e - WEEK)
        else:
            starts.append(s)
            ends.append(e)
    starts.sort()
    ends.sort()
    out = []
    for t in orders:
        t %= WEEK
        # opened at or before t, minus closed at or before t
        out.append(bisect_right(starts, t) - bisect_right(ends, t))
    return out

Explanation. Every interval becomes a half-open range [s, e) on a line of 10 080 week minutes. An interval that closes before it opens ends on the next day, and if that runs past Sunday midnight the piece after it wraps to Monday morning. At minute t, the intervals that contain t are exactly those that started at or before t minus those that also ended at or before t (every interval that has ended has also started). With the starts and the ends sorted separately, both counts are bisect_right. Reducing t modulo the week handles orders in later weeks. Because a store's own intervals never overlap, open intervals equal open stores, and an all-day store written as seven (day, 0, 1440) intervals contributes exactly one at midnight: one interval ends at t while the next starts there.

Complexity. O(n log n) to sort and O(log n) per order: O((n + q) log n). The timing test (about 22 000 intervals, 20 000 orders) runs in about 0.03 s in CPython. Checking every interval for every order is about 40 s.

The middle approach. The most likely middle solution sorts the intervals by start and, per order, scans from the beginning until the starts pass t, counting those that have not ended. It is still O(n) per order (half the list on average) and takes about 14 to 17 s on the timing test, so it fails the 8 s limit. A precomputed count for every minute of the week (a difference array of +1 at each start and −1 at each end, then a prefix sum over 10 080 minutes) is O(n + W + q), passes easily and is an excellent answer if the candidate states that it depends on the week having a small, fixed number of minutes. An interval tree also passes but is more than the problem needs.

Dialect notes. In Java, two int[] arrays with Arrays.sort and a hand-written upper-bound binary search. In SQL, the same count is a range join of orders to intervals (ON t >= s AND t < e) with a GROUP BY, which is O(n·q) unless the engine has an interval or range-join optimisation; the scalable SQL version is a running sum over a union of +1/−1 events joined back by time. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. An order at the opening minute (open) and at the closing minute (closed); the gap between lunch and dinner; hours on one day not applying to the next; minutes 0 and 10 079; several stores open at once with one closing on the order's minute. Hard: an interval across midnight at 23:59, 00:00, its last minute and its close; Sunday night into Monday morning of the same week; a close of 0 and a close of 1440 on the same day. Very Hard: orders in later weeks; a 24-hour store as adjacent days at midnight; Sunday night into Monday of a later week.

Common mistakes. Closed intervals (t <= e), which count a store at its closing minute and twice at midnight for an all-day store; treating close < open as a mistake or as same-day; forgetting the wrap from Sunday into Monday; bisect_left on the ends; not reducing later-week orders modulo the week; checking every interval per order.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Keep intervals sorted by start with their ends, or a per-minute list of open store ids for a small W; listing k open stores costs at least O(k). (2) Holiday hours replace a date's weekly hours: put intervals on a calendar line for the period instead of the repeating week, built from weekly hours minus replaced dates plus holiday intervals; the two-bisect query stays the same. (3) Pauses are subtractions: count pauses that contain t with the same two-bisect trick and subtract, provided a pause lies inside open hours (state the assumption, otherwise clip pauses to hours first). (4) For a stream, keep the sorted starts and ends (or the per-minute counts) and rebuild only for the store whose hours changed: remove its old intervals and add the new ones (O(n) with lists, O(log n) with a balanced tree or a Fenwick tree over minutes).

Rubric anchors. 2: a scan per order, or the closing-minute and midnight rules wrong. 3: all tests pass with two bisects or a per-minute count array. 4: also explains why starts minus ends counts open intervals and handles holiday hours and pauses credibly.

def repeat_carts(orders):
    last = {}                      # (account, canonical cart) -> most recent order_id
    out = []
    for order_id, account, lines in orders:
        qty = {}
        for line in lines:
            item, q = line[0], line[1]
            opts = tuple(sorted(line[2])) if len(line) > 2 else ()
            qty[(item, opts)] = qty.get((item, opts), 0) + q
        cart = tuple(sorted((k, q) for k, q in qty.items() if q > 0))
        if not cart:
            out.append(None)
            continue
        key = (account, cart)
        out.append(last.get(key))
        last[key] = order_id
    return out

Explanation. A cart is a multiset of lines, so its canonical form is: add up quantities per line key (the item, with its options sorted so their order does not matter), drop zero quantities, and sort. The sorted tuple is hashable, so (account, cart) keys a dictionary whose value is the most recent order with that cart; looking it up before storing the current order gives "the most recent earlier match". An order with no positive line has an empty cart, returns None and is never stored, so it can never match. Below Very Hard, opts is always (), and below Hard there are no repeated items or zero lines, so the same code serves every level.

Complexity. O(m log m) per order for its own m lines plus O(m) hashing: O(Σ m log m) overall, independent of how many orders an account has. O(distinct carts) memory. The timing test (two accounts with 25 000 orders each, or 18 000 at Very Hard) runs in about 0.2 to 0.35 s in CPython. Comparing each order with every earlier one of the account, rebuilding the earlier carts each time, takes minutes.

The middle approach. The most likely middle solution builds the same canonical tuple but keeps a per-account list of earlier carts and tests cart in earlier, then walks back to find the most recent match. Although in runs in C and tuple comparison stops early on a length mismatch, it is still O(k) per order, O(k²) per account: on the timing test it takes about 25 to 50 s depending on the level, so it fails the 8 s limit. The test is sized for that: the heavy accounts have tens of thousands of orders, and carts repeat about one time in ten, so most in tests scan the whole list. Keying a dict on a sorted string or a frozenset of (item, quantity) pairs (with quantities summed first) is also O(1) per lookup and accepted.

Dialect notes. In Java, build a canonical String (or a List<Map.Entry> with proper equals/hashCode) after sorting; a HashMap<String, Integer> per line key first. In SQL, the canonical cart is STRING_AGG(item_id || ':' || qty, ',' ORDER BY item_id) per order after summing quantities, and the most recent earlier match is LAG(order_id) OVER (PARTITION BY account_id, cart ORDER BY placed_at). Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. The same lines in another order (a repeat); a different quantity (not); another account's identical cart (not); two earlier matches (the most recent is returned); a subset of an earlier cart (not). Hard: the same item on two lines adding up to an earlier single line; a zero-quantity line ignored; empty carts returning None and never matching. Very Hard: options in another order (same line); the same item with different options (different lines), including a split that adds up to the same cart; an empty options tuple equal to no options.

Common mistakes. Comparing raw line lists; a set of items, which loses quantities; a frozenset of lines before summing repeated items; returning the first earlier match rather than the most recent; storing the order before looking up, which makes every order match itself; matching across accounts; treating an empty cart as a cart that can match; Counter objects used as dictionary keys (they are unhashable), or zero quantities kept in the key.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Near repeats: index each cart under each of its "one line removed" variants (O(m) keys per cart) and look up the current cart and its own variants; or use MinHash for similarity, stated as approximate. (2) Key on a stable catalogue identifier (a master item behind the menu item), with a mapping table versioned by date; risks are wrong merges and lost matches across the rebuild. (3) Keep the dictionary of the latest order per (account, cart) as state, or a table of it; it grows with distinct carts, so expire carts not seen for a stated period. (4) See the dialect notes: a canonical string per order, then LAG within (account, cart).

Rubric anchors. 2: compares against every earlier order, or ignores quantities or line order. 3: all tests pass with a canonical key in a dictionary. 4: also explains why in on a list is quadratic despite running in C, and gives good answers on near repeats and changing ids.

def most_lines_filled(orders):
    out = []
    for order in orders:
        reserved = order.get("reserved", {})
        cap = {}                                   # spare units per item, after in-stock lines
        for item, n in order["units"].items():
            left = n - reserved.get(item, 0)
            if left > 0:
                cap[item] = left
        # Approved items the store can actually supply, each listed once.
        approved = [list(dict.fromkeys(a for a in items if a in cap)) for _line, items in order["lines"]]
        holders = {item: [] for item in cap}       # item -> lines currently filled by it

        def place(i, seen):
            """Fill line i, moving other lines along an augmenting path if needed."""
            for item in approved[i]:
                if item in seen:
                    continue
                seen.add(item)
                h = holders[item]
                if len(h) < cap[item]:             # a spare unit: take it
                    h.append(i)
                    return True
                for j, other in enumerate(h):      # full: can a holder move elsewhere?
                    if place(other, seen):
                        h[j] = i
                        return True
            return False

        filled = 0
        for i in range(len(approved)):
            if approved[i] and place(i, set()):
                filled += 1
        out.append(filled)
    return out

Explanation. Lines and items form a bipartite graph, with an item allowed as many lines as it has spare units. This is a maximum matching with capacities on one side (equivalently, a maximum flow from a source through lines, with capacity 1, and items, with capacity = spare units, to a sink). Kuhn's algorithm adds lines one at a time. For each line it searches depth first for an augmenting path: take an item with a spare unit, or take a full item and recursively move one of its current holders to another item that holder approves. The visited set of items makes each search O(E). A line that finds no path now never finds one later in the same order (Berge's theorem: the matching is maximum when no augmenting path exists, and a line that cannot be added cannot become addable by adding further lines). Spare units are units minus reserved units, floored at zero; repeated and unstocked items are dropped from approved lists before the search.

Complexity. O(L · E) per order in the worst case for L lines and E approved pairs, usually far less; O(L + E) memory. The timing test (1 500 orders of 20 to 40 lines, or 30 to 60 lines at Hard and Very Hard) takes 0.08–0.13 s in CPython. Trying every assignment (backtracking over each line's approved items, with the bound "filled + lines left cannot beat the best") took more than a second on 34 of the first 60 orders of a 40-line test and on all of the first 60 orders of a 60-line test; one 40-line order ran for over a minute. The whole test would take far longer than the 8 s limit.

The likely middle approach, and why the timing test is not what catches it. Greedy first fit (lines in order, each takes its first approved item with a unit left) is O(E) and very fast, and it is wrong: it can use up the only item another line accepts. Every seeded sample contains at least one order where first fit fills fewer lines than the maximum, and the checks include a two-line counterexample, an order where "fewest options first" also fails (every line has two options), and a six-line chain where every line must move to its second choice. Greedy therefore fails the samples and checks, and the timing test only confirms it (the timing test compares with the reference, and first fit fills fewer lines on two thirds or more of its orders). A max-flow implementation (Edmonds–Karp or Dinic) is a correct alternative and passes comfortably at these sizes; Hopcroft–Karp is faster in theory and unnecessary here.

Dialect notes. In Java, Scala or C++ the same DFS uses arrays indexed by line and item number (map ids to integers first) and an int array per item for holders; recursion depth is at most the number of lines, which is small. In SQL there is no practical formulation of augmenting paths; a set-based greedy is the best SQL offers and it has the same flaw. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. First fit blocking a line with one choice; a tie where fewest-options-first still fails; a long chain of moves; an item with two units filling two lines; approved items with zero units or no entry; empty approved lists (refunds); an item repeated in one approved list; more units than lines; several orders whose units must not be shared, including an order with no lines; (Very Hard) reserved units taken off first, more reserved than on hand (zero, never negative), and a reservation for an item no line approves.

Common mistakes. Greedy in any order; counting an item with three units as one; letting units leak between orders; counting a repeated item twice in the visited logic or the capacity; a negative spare count after reservations, which breaks len(h) < cap comparisons; forgetting the visited set, which makes the search exponential or infinite; returning the assignment instead of the count, or the count of filled items instead of lines.

Follow-up guidance. (1) First fit: [[a, b], [a]] with one unit each. Fewest first: four lines [c, d], [a, d], [b, d], [b, c] with one unit each; all have two options, input order breaks the tie, and greedy fills three of four. (2) This becomes a minimum-cost maximum flow (or the Hungarian method with ranks as costs and a large reward per filled line); a cheaper approximation is to try first choices first in each DFS, which is a heuristic, not a guarantee. (3) A budget per order makes it a constrained problem: maximise lines subject to total extra cost, which is no longer a plain matching (it is a min-cost flow with a budget, or an integer program); with tiny orders, search is fine. (4) Show "up to N lines" rather than a promise, re-run the matching whenever a shelf turns out empty (only that item's holders need to move), and record what was found, substituted or refunded per line.

Rubric anchors. 2: greedy or every-assignment search, correct on some samples only. 3: all checks pass with augmenting paths or max flow, capacities and reservations right. 4: also gives a small counterexample to greedy unprompted, argues why a line that fails once never needs retrying, states the complexity, and answers the preference follow-up with min-cost flow.

Strong signals. Recognises bipartite matching quickly; asks whether units are per item and shared across lines; builds a counterexample before coding. Red flags. "Sort by fewest options and it's always optimal"; trying every assignment with no estimate of its cost.

import heapq


def price_timeline(base, promotions, horizon):
    starts = {item: [] for item in base}
    for created, (pid, item, start, end, price) in enumerate(promotions):
        start, end = max(start, 0), min(end, horizon)     # only the part inside the period
        if start < end:
            starts[item].append((start, price, created, end, pid))
    out = {}
    for item, rows in base.items():
        promos = sorted(starts[item])
        changes = sorted(rows)
        times = sorted({0} | {p[0] for p in promos} | {p[3] for p in promos if p[3] < horizon}
                       | {t for t, _ in changes if 0 <= t < horizon})
        heap, segs = [], []
        pi = ci = 0
        cur_base = None
        for t in times:
            while ci < len(changes) and changes[ci][0] <= t:
                cur_base = changes[ci][1]
                ci += 1
            while pi < len(promos) and promos[pi][0] == t:
                _s, price, created, end, pid = promos[pi]
                heapq.heappush(heap, (price, created, end, pid))   # cheapest, then oldest
                pi += 1
            while heap and heap[0][2] <= t:                         # lazy deletion of ended ones
                heapq.heappop(heap)
            if heap and heap[0][0] < cur_base:
                state = (heap[0][0], heap[0][3])
            else:
                state = (cur_base, None)
            if segs and (segs[-1][2], segs[-1][3]) == state:
                continue                                            # nothing visible changed
            if segs:
                segs[-1][1] = t
            segs.append([t, horizon, state[0], state[1]])
        out[item] = [tuple(s) for s in segs]
    return out

Explanation. The winner can only change at a promotion's start or end, or at a base price change, so the sweep visits those times in order. Active promotions sit in a min-heap keyed by (price, creation index), so the top is the cheapest and, among equal prices, the oldest. Ended promotions are not removed when they end; each one stays in the heap until it reaches the top, and is popped then (lazy deletion). Only the top matters, so a stale entry lower down is harmless. The top wins only if it is strictly below the base price in force; otherwise the base price shows with no promotion. A segment is opened only when (price, promotion) changes, which merges pieces where the same promotion keeps winning across a base change or across another promotion's start or end. Clipping to [0, horizon) happens before anything else, and a promotion entirely outside the period disappears.

Complexity. O(n log n) per item for n promotions (sorting plus one push and at most one pop each) and O(n) memory. The timing test (80 000 promotions on four items over four weeks of minutes, thousands active at once) takes 0.31–0.49 s in CPython. Evaluating every promotion at every boundary (O(n²) per item) extrapolates to 160–210 s.

The middle approach. A sweep that keeps a plain list of active promotions, removes ended ones with list.remove and takes min() of the list at each boundary is O(n · a) for a active. With thousands active it took 18.6–24.3 s on the timing test, so it fails the 8 s limit. A sorted list maintained with bisect.insort and deleting by bisect does O(log a) comparisons per update but moves O(a) pointers in C; it took 1.05 s and passes. Accept it as a correct O(n log n)-comparison method, and ask about memory moves (a follow-up rule fires on insort). A balanced tree or SortedList is equivalent.

Dialect notes. In Java use a PriorityQueue with a comparator on price then creation index, and the same lazy pop; a TreeSet supports removal directly. In SQL, segments come from cutting at every start, end and base change (a UNION of boundary times, LEAD for the next boundary), then a lateral join that picks ORDER BY price, created LIMIT 1 per piece, and finally gaps-and-islands to merge pieces with the same winner. That is correct and set-based but O(pieces × active) without a suitable index. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. Overlapping promotions; equal prices where the older promotion started later (and the change of winner at equal price opens a new segment); a promotion ending exactly when another starts; the next best returning when the cheapest ends; a dearer promotion inside the winner (no split); an item with no promotions next to an item with one; clipping at both ends and a promotion starting at the horizon; a promotion at the base price; (Very Hard) a lower new base that beats a running promotion, a winner that survives a base change as one segment, a base row with an unchanged price, and a base rise that lets a promotion win from that moment.

Common mistakes. Breaking ties by start time instead of creation order; merging adjacent segments by price only; letting a promotion at the base price win; closed ranges; forgetting to clip; removing ended promotions eagerly from a list; re-sorting the active set at every boundary; producing per-minute output.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Keep each item's segment starts in a sorted array and bisect per lookup (O(log s)), or join orders to segments in a warehouse on start <= t < end. (2) A percentage promotion's price depends on the base, so its heap key changes at base changes; recompute the active keys at each base change (they are few), or key by percentage within a base period. (3) Version the promotion set: store the timeline "as shown" with the promotions known at the time, and a recomputed "as now" timeline, each with a computed-at stamp; never rewrite what was shown. (4) Only the item's segments overlapping [start, end) of the new promotion can change; recompute that window from the active set at its start.

Rubric anchors. 2: per-minute evaluation or a list rescan, or tie and merge rules wrong. 3: all checks pass with a heap sweep or sorted structure, ties by creation order. 4: also explains lazy deletion and why only the top matters, gives the costs of the middle approaches, and answers the percentage and incremental follow-ups concretely.

Strong signals. Asks what "older" means before sorting; notices that a change of winner at equal price is still a change. Red flags. Output per minute "to be safe"; dropping the promotion id from the output.

import math
from fractions import Fraction


def _half_up(x):
    """An exact amount in cents -> whole cents, halves rounded up."""
    return math.floor(x + Fraction(1, 2))


def price_carts(carts, fees):
    out = []
    for cart in carts:
        subtotal = 0
        item_discount = Fraction(0)
        for line in cart["lines"]:
            mods = sum(m["price"] for m in line.get("modifiers", []))
            line_total = (line["price"] + mods) * line["qty"]                       # modifiers per unit
            subtotal += line_total
            item_discount += Fraction(line_total * line.get("promo_pct", 0), 100)   # exact, no rounding yet
        order_discount = Fraction(0)
        promo = cart.get("order_promo")
        if promo:
            after_items = subtotal - item_discount                                  # item promotions first
            order_discount = min(Fraction(promo["max_off"]), after_items * promo["pct"] / 100)
        discounted = _half_up(subtotal - item_discount - order_discount)            # the one rounding
        delivery = fees["delivery"]
        if cart["member"] and subtotal >= fees["member_min"]:                       # before promotions
            delivery = 0
        tax = _half_up(Fraction(discounted * fees["tax_bps"], 10000))               # on the discounted subtotal
        out.append({"subtotal": subtotal, "discount": subtotal - discounted, "delivery_fee": delivery,
                    "tax": tax, "total": discounted + delivery + tax})
    return out

The planted bugs, their symptoms and their fixes.

  1. Modifiers are charged once per line. price * qty + mods. Symptom: two burgers with extra cheese pay for the cheese once. Fix: (price + mods) * qty.
  2. The order promotion is taken from the subtotal before item promotions. Symptom: an item on promotion plus a 20% code gives 20% of the undiscounted subtotal, more than the code allows. Fix: take pct of subtotal - item_discount, then apply the cap.
  3. The membership waiver tests the discounted subtotal. Symptom: a member whose items are above the minimum is charged delivery after a code brings the total below it. Fix: test subtotal (before promotions), this exercise's rule.
  4. Tax is charged on the subtotal before promotions. Symptom: tax too high on every discounted order. Fix: tax the rounded discounted subtotal.
  5. Each line's discount is rounded down on its own. line_total * pct // 100. Symptom: carts with several discounted lines are a cent or more too high. Fix: keep each discount exact (a Fraction) and round once.

Each bug has its own check in which the others do not show: a modifier on a quantity of two with no promotions (bug 1); an item promotion plus an order code with tax at 0 and whole-cent discounts (bug 2); a member at 1 500 with a 25% code and a 1 200 minimum, no item promotions, tax 0 (bug 3); a 10% item promotion with 8% tax and a whole-cent discount (bug 4); two lines of 1 005 at 10%, tax 0 (bug 5). Three checks pass on the original code and guard the fixes: half a cent rounds up (904.5 → 905, so a fix with Python's round(), which gives 904, fails), the order promotion's cap, and a member exactly at the minimum next to a non-member.

Explanation. Pricing is a fixed order of operations on exact amounts: line totals with per-unit modifiers, item promotions, the capped order promotion on what remains, one rounding to cents, then the fee rule (on the cart before promotions) and tax (on the discounted subtotal). Rounding once means discounts are carried as exact fractions until the discounted subtotal is stated.

Complexity. O(total lines) time and O(carts) output. The timing test is 30 000 carts; the fixed code takes about 0.42–0.44 s in CPython with Fraction. An integer version (amounts scaled by 100 and 10 000) takes about a quarter of that and is equally correct.

Dialect notes. In SQL, compute line totals and exact discounts in NUMERIC, sum per cart, apply LEAST(max_off, after_items * pct / 100), and round once with ROUND(x) in PostgreSQL (NUMERIC rounds halves away from zero, which is "halves up" for positive amounts); BigQuery's ROUND on NUMERIC behaves the same, while FLOAT64 does not. In Java use BigDecimal with RoundingMode.HALF_UP, never double. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. A modifier on quantity two; an item promotion plus an order code; a member above the minimum before promotions and below it after; tax on a discounted cart; fractional discounts on two lines; a half cent; the order promotion's cap; a member exactly at the minimum and a non-member.

Common mistakes. Fixing rounding with round() (banker's rounding) or floats; rounding the tax on the unrounded subtotal and getting a different cent; applying the order promotion's cap before computing its percentage; moving the waiver test but keeping the discounted subtotal; rewriting the function instead of fixing it.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Say which subtotal it tests and keep both rules in one place, with the consumer shown why a code or the waiver applied. (2) Allocate the order discount and tax to lines in proportion to line amounts, with the rounding remainder assigned by a stated rule (largest remainder) so line refunds sum to what was charged. (3) Tax per line by tax category, then round per tax rate or per line as the rule requires; the output gains a tax breakdown. (4) One pricing library (or service) used by both, versioned rules, and a stored price breakdown at checkout that the charge reuses rather than recomputes.

Rubric anchors. 2: finds two or three bugs, some checks still fail. 3: all five fixed, all checks pass, each explained. 4: also explains each symptom from the consumer's side, keeps exact arithmetic with a single rounding, and answers the refund-allocation follow-up concretely.

Strong signals. Works the hint by hand; asks which subtotal the waiver uses before changing it. Red flags. Converting to floats "to simplify"; rounding each line "because receipts show lines".

DSH-L2-04.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Intake. One endpoint (or poller) per point-of-sale kind writes raw payloads unchanged to object storage and a log keyed by store, with received_at, the integration's own sequence or timestamp, and a payload hash. Adapters map each format to a canonical model: menu (store_id, version), category, item (store_id, item_key, external_id, name, price_minor, tax_category), modifier_group (min, max), modifier_option, menu_hours, plus availability (store_id, item_key, available, as_of).
  • Two paths. Full menus and structural changes go through validation and versioned publishing; price and availability updates take a fast path that patches the current published version within {{freshness}}. Each update carries the source's sequence or timestamp; an update older than what is applied for that field is ignored (per-field last-applied stamps), so a late full menu cannot undo a newer sold-out flag.
  • Dedup. A normalised full menu (sorted keys, canonical ordering) is hashed; an unchanged resend is acknowledged and dropped.
  • Validation. Schema checks, price sanity (zero, negative, a hundredfold change), modifier groups whose minimum exceeds their options, orphan items, and a size guard (a menu that drops more than a stated share of items is held). Failing menus go to quarantine; the last good version stays live; the merchant sees the reason in their own tools.
  • Publishing. A new menu version is written completely and then made current with one pointer switch; caches and the search index are updated from a change event; rollback is a pointer switch back.
  • Identity. A stable item_key per store, mapped from external ids, with a matching step (name, price, category) when a rebuild changes every external id; history, ratings and reports use item_key.
  • Observability. Per integration and per store: last update received, time from receipt to publish, validation failure rate, quarantine count, and stores with no update in an expected interval. Merchants see only their own stores.
  • History. Every published version is kept (or stored as SCD type 2 rows), so "the menu at 18:30 last Friday" is the version current then, plus availability changes as of that time.

Competing designs to accept. Event-sourcing every menu change; documents per store menu in a document store with versions; separate services for structure and availability. All fine if ordering, validation with last-good fallback and atomic publishing are explicit.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Full-menu resends flooding search reindexing (fixed by hashing and diffs); one slow adapter blocking others (separate queues per integration); out-of-order updates without per-field stamps; non-atomic publishes showing half a menu; caches invalidated by TTL only.

Incident guidance.

  • Prices arrive in dollars instead of cents from one point-of-sale kind: a price sanity check comparing to the last published price (a hundredfold drop) should have quarantined them. Roll the affected stores back to the last good version, block orders at the wrong prices, fix the adapter, and add the ratio check to validation for every integration. Report affected orders to merchants.
  • A full menu with every modifier group missing is published: validation should hold a menu that loses required modifier groups (items with required groups now without them). Roll back by pointer switch; add a structural diff guard (share of items losing groups) and alert the integration's owner.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Hash and drop unchanged resends; index only the diff. (2) Map new external ids to stable item keys by matching and confirm uncertain matches with the merchant. (3) Hold, notify the merchant and publish on confirmation; a size guard is the evidence. (4) Keep it as a pending availability fact with its timestamp, applied when the item appears if still newer. (5) Keep every version with its validity interval and availability changes with timestamps.

Rubric anchors. 2: overwrite the menu on every payload; no validation or versions. 3: canonical model, validation with quarantine, versioned atomic publishing, a fast path for availability. 4: also per-field ordering against late full menus, hashing for resends, stable identity across rebuilds, and concrete incident fixes tied to validation rules.

Strong signals. Separates availability from structure; asks how merchants learn about rejected menus. Red flags. Publishing whatever arrives; deleting the previous version.

DSH-L2-05.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Quotes. POST /quotes with the merchant's order reference, addresses, items summary and channel returns a stored quote (quote_id, merchant_id, fee_minor, eta, expires_at = now + {{quote_ttl}}, channel).
  • Acceptance. POST /deliveries with quote_id and an idempotency key. The first request creates delivery (delivery_id, quote_id, merchant_id, external_ref, state, version); a retry with the same key returns the same response; the same key with a different body returns a conflict; an expired quote returns a clear error and asks for a new quote. A unique constraint on quote_id stops two deliveries for one quote.
  • State. States ranked created < courier assigned < picked up < delivered, with cancelled as a terminal state from any non-terminal state. Events from the delivery service are applied only if they move the state forward; out-of-order events are recorded but do not move it back. Every change increments version.
  • Webhooks. A transactional outbox writes one row per state change; a sender delivers with retries and exponential backoff per merchant endpoint, with delivery_id, state, version and occurred_at, so merchants can drop older versions. After a stated retry period, updates are marked undelivered and the merchant is alerted. GET /deliveries/{id} is the source of truth for recovery.
  • Cancellations and charges. Rules by state (this exercise's rules): free before courier assignment, a fee after pickup; each cancellation records who cancelled and why.
  • Reporting. fct_delivery (merchant_id, channel, day, state, fee_minor, times between states) in a warehouse, refreshed often; merchants query only their own rows (row-level security by merchant). Courier details shown during a delivery are minimal and expire; reports show only aggregates such as median pickup-to-delivery time.

Competing designs to accept. Polling-only for small merchants; a streaming state store instead of a relational table; server-sent events instead of webhooks. Fine if idempotent acceptance, ordered state and recovery are explicit.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Webhook senders blocked by one slow endpoint (isolate per endpoint); retries without backoff overwhelming a recovering merchant; out-of-order events regressing state; quotes stored forever ({{daily_requests}} a day, most never accepted: keep briefly, aggregate for conversion reporting).

Incident guidance.

  • A retry bug accepts every quote twice: idempotency keys and a unique constraint on quote_id make the second acceptance return the first delivery; without them, cancel the duplicates before assignment, refund, and add the constraint. Alert on deliveries per external reference above one.
  • The webhook sender falls six hours behind: the outbox keeps every update; drain it with per-endpoint parallelism, and send only the latest version per delivery when far behind. Tell merchants to reconcile with the query endpoint; add a lag monitor and alert before it reaches minutes.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Same key: one delivery, the same response twice. (2) Outbox retries with backoff; after recovery, the merchant receives the latest state per delivery (or all versions, marked) and can query to reconcile. (3) A cancellation event after pickup, the fee by this exercise's rule, a report row in cancelled state with the reason. (4) Delivery durations per channel from your timestamps; the merchant's own pickup times stay on their side; no individual courier data. (5) Keep quotes for days, aggregate quote-to-acceptance by channel for the merchant, then delete.

Rubric anchors. 2: synchronous calls with no idempotency, fire-and-forget webhooks. 3: stored quotes with expiry, idempotent acceptance, a forward-only state machine, an outbox with retries and a query endpoint, per-merchant reports. 4: also cancellation and charge rules by state, per-endpoint isolation, minimal and expiring courier data, and concrete incident plans.

Strong signals. Asks what identifies a retry; designs recovery around a query endpoint. Red flags. Exposing courier history to merchants; webhooks as the only source of truth.

DSH-L3-01.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Stable identity. menu_items (item_key, store_id, created_at) is the marketplace's own key; item_source_ids (item_key, source, source_item_id, valid_from, valid_to) maps point-of-sale ids to it over time. A re-sync matches incoming items to existing keys (source id first, then name + category + price similarity with review for low-confidence matches) instead of minting new keys.
  • Structure and versions. Nodes: menus (menu_id, store_id), categories, items, modifier_groups (group_id, store_id), options (option_id, group_id). Each node has a version table with valid_from, valid_to, recorded_at: item_versions (item_key, version, name, description, base_flag_in_stock), group_versions (group_id, version, name, min_select, max_select), option_versions (option_id, version, name, price_delta_cents, nested_group_id NULL). Edges are versioned too: menu_category_items (menu_id, category_id, item_key, position, valid_from, valid_to), item_groups (item_key, group_id, position, valid_from, valid_to). A shared group is one group_id referenced by many item_groups rows; editing it writes one new group or option version.
  • Hours and prices. menu_hours (menu_id, iso_weekday, open_local, close_local, valid_from, valid_to) in store-local time. prices (item_key, menu_id, channel, amount_cents, valid_from, valid_to) so lunch and dinner prices and channel prices (on {{channel_list}}) are rows, not columns; the precedence when two open menus list the item (this exercise: the menu that opened later wins) lives in the resolution function and is recorded with a rule version.
  • Published versions. Optionally, each change also produces an immutable published_menu (store_id, channel, version, published_at, content_hash, document) used for serving; it is derived from the node versions, not the source of truth.
  • Orders. order_lines (order_line_id, item_key, item_version, menu_id, channel, unit_price_cents) and order_line_options (order_line_id, path, option_id, option_version, group_id, group_version, price_delta_cents, name_at_order); a frozen name and price per option means receipts and refunds never depend on the live menu.
  • Menu as of T. Filter every version and edge table by valid_from <= T < valid_to for the store and channel, and evaluate menu hours at T in local time. Or, with published versions, take the latest published_at <= T.
  • Validation. For each group attached at a level, count selected options: min_select <= n <= max_select; recurse into the nested group of each selected option only; a nested group under an unselected option is ignored even if min_select > 0. Depth ≤ 3 and a cycle check (a group may not appear on its own path) at write time.

Competing designs to accept. Immutable published-menu documents per change as the only store, with a normalised index derived for analytics, if the candidate costs the storage (a full copy of {{items_per_menu}} items per change) and explains how history questions are answered. A bitemporal node model. An event-sourced menu log with projections. A document store for serving plus versioned relational tables for history.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Point-of-sale ids as keys; prices overwritten in place; order lines pointing at live nodes; a whole-menu rewrite per change at {{menu_changes}} changes a day; validation that treats nested required groups as always required; menu hours stored in UTC with a fixed offset; no rule for two open menus listing the same item.

Incident guidance.

  • Re-sync made every item new: item keys must be the marketplace's own. Rebuild item_source_ids by matching the new point-of-sale ids to the old keys (exact matches first, review the rest), re-point the new rows to the old keys, and merge the reset history; add a check that a re-sync creating more than a small share of new items is held for review.
  • Shared group edit changed old receipts: order lines referenced live nodes. Rebuild the past from version history where it exists (option versions valid at order time), freeze names and prices on order lines going forward, and recompute the refunds issued with the wrong amounts.
  • Publishing fell behind: rebuilding whole menus per change does not scale. Publish incrementally (only the changed items and the items sharing a changed group), coalesce changes per store within a short window, and alert on publish lag rather than discovering stale prices from consumers.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Recursive check over selected options; required nested groups only under selected parents; reject selections of options not in the group version valid at order time. (2) One new option version and one new group version (if max changes); no item rows change; the earlier order shows its frozen options. (3) Mapping table from source ids to stable keys; a re-sync writes new mapping rows. (4) Snapshot: changes × items per menu rows (or bytes) per day, cheap "as of" reads; node versions: rows proportional to changes, "as of" needs a join over versions per node; many teams do both. (5) Resolution rule with a version, applied per channel; the order line stores the menu and price used.

Rubric anchors. 2: one item table with a price column and a JSON blob of modifiers, updated in place; order lines reference live items. 3: versioned nodes or published snapshots, shared groups, channel prices, frozen order lines, correct validation. 4: also stable identity across re-syncs, explicit precedence for overlapping menus, storage and publish costs estimated, cycle and depth checks, incident repairs from history.

Strong signals. Asks how a shared group's change propagates; freezes order lines unprompted; separates the serving document from the source of truth. Red flags. Point-of-sale ids as primary keys; receipts rebuilt from the live menu; money as floating point.

DSH-L3-02.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design).

  • Stores and zones. stores (store_id, time_zone_iana); store_time_zone_history (store_id, time_zone_iana, valid_from, valid_to, is_correction). A correction re-derives intervals; whether past answers move is a stated choice (usually: the corrected zone applies to the past too, with the old answers kept in a log of what was served).
  • Schedules. schedule_versions (schedule_id, store_id, valid_from_utc, valid_to_utc, saved_at, source) and schedule_intervals (schedule_id, iso_weekday, open_local TIME, close_local TIME, is_24h): close earlier than open means the next day; is_24h is an explicit flag, so an equal open and close is rejected as an error. An edit creates a new version effective from the save instant; past versions are never changed.
  • Overrides. date_overrides (override_id, store_id, local_date, kind closed|hours, open_local, close_local, saved_at, superseded_at): replaces only the intervals that open on that local date.
  • Pauses. pauses (pause_id, store_id, started_at_utc, planned_end_utc NULL, ended_at_utc NULL, started_by merchant|system_device_offline, ended_by merchant|system|expiry). A merchant pause and an automatic pause can coexist; the store reopens only when no pause is active.
  • Resolution at instant T. Convert T to the store's local time with the zone in force; candidate dates are the local date and the day before; for each, take the override if one exists, else the schedule version in force, and turn its intervals into UTC instants with the IANA zone rules (wall-clock honoured: on a fall-back night 22:00–02:00 lasts 5 hours, on a spring-forward night 3). Open if T is in an interval and no pause is active; the reason code says which source decided.
  • Derived table. open_intervals (store_id, opens_at_utc, closes_at_utc, source_version, derived_at) for the next N weeks, regenerated per store on every schedule edit, override, zone change and as the horizon rolls; "open now" = an interval lookup minus active pauses held in a fast key-value store keyed by store. At {{open_checks}} checks a second, serving reads a cache or in-memory index per region; pause starts and ends are pushed (events) rather than polled, with a freshness target in seconds.
  • History. Because versions and pauses are append-only, "was S open at T" replays resolution with the versions valid at T; the derived intervals are also kept (not deleted) so past answers are cheap.

Competing designs to accept. Computing open/closed on read with no derived table, if the candidate shows the read cost fits {{open_checks}} checks a second with caching. Storing intervals as tstzrange with exclusion constraints. An RRULE-style recurrence representation, if overnight intervals and overrides are handled.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Fixed UTC offsets; a single boolean "open now" refreshed by a job; holiday edits written into the weekly schedule; overrides that cut the previous night's late shift; pauses with no source, so automatic pauses cannot end automatically; open-ended pauses without monitoring; past answers that change when hours are edited.

Incident guidance.

  • Closed for the last hour on fall-back night: intervals were derived with a fixed offset. Re-derive with IANA zone rules across the {{time_zones}} zones, add tests for both transition nights, and compare derived durations with listed wall-clock durations each night before a transition.
  • Holiday saved as a weekly change: the edit path did not distinguish an override from a schedule change. Restore the prior schedule version as a new version effective immediately, re-enter the holiday as a date override, re-derive intervals, and add a confirmation (or a separate UI path) for edits that affect every future week.
  • Automatic pauses stuck after an outage: automatic pauses must carry their source and end when the device reconnects. Close the stuck pauses with ended_by = system, alert on pause starts above the normal rate ({{pauses_per_day}} a day is the baseline), and report lost open minutes to the affected merchants.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Local date and previous date; override else schedule; UTC conversion; pause check; reason code. (2) Spring forward: 22:00–02:00 holds 3 elapsed hours; fall back: 5; the interval endpoints are what the zone rules give for those wall-clock times. (3) A new schedule version from Friday's save instant; derived rows from then on change; last Saturday answers from the old version. (4) Derived intervals regionally replicated, pauses pushed to the serving cache in seconds. (5) The scheduled orders table joined to overrides saved after the orders were placed; the order should be flagged for the merchant and the consumer (this exercise's rule decides whether it is cancelled).

Rubric anchors. 2: hours as text or a single open/close per day; a boolean open flag; UTC offsets. 3: schedule, overrides and pauses separated; overnight intervals; IANA time zones; derived intervals. 4: also versioned history for past instants, daylight-saving behaviour stated and handled, pause sources and open-ended pauses, serving design sized, incidents repaired.

Strong signals. Asks immediately about midnight and daylight saving; keeps "the rule" separate from "the derived intervals". Red flags. Storing UTC offsets; overwriting hours; treating a holiday as a weekly change.

DSH-L3-03.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design).

  • Master catalogue. master_items (master_item_id, family_id, brand, name, size_value, size_unit, unit_kind each|weight, created_at); product_families (family_id) links a can and a 6-pack. master_item_codes (master_item_id, code, code_type barcode|store_code, valid_from, valid_to): a barcode is an attribute with a validity, not the key, so a reused barcode points to a new master item from a date.
  • Listings. listings (listing_id, store_id, merchant_item_id, first_seen_at); listing_versions (listing_id, version, name, size_text, price_cents, price_unit each|kg|lb, valid_from, valid_to, feed_batch_id) written only when an attribute changes (hash compare). A reused merchant id with a different product closes the old listing and opens a new one (detected by a large change in name, size or barcode).
  • Mapping. listing_mappings (listing_id, master_item_id, source barcode|manual|model, confidence, valid_from, valid_to, recorded_at, superseded_by); a correction is a new row superseding the old, so reports can be restated for the period. Low-confidence matches go to a review queue; units are normalised (oz to ml, counts) before matching.
  • Signals. availability_signals (listing_id, observed_at, recorded_at, source feed|pick|sale, value in_stock|out_of_stock|found|not_found, quantity NULL), append-only; no state is stored here.
  • Orders. order_lines (order_line_id, order_id, listing_id, listing_version, master_item_id_at_order, ordered_qty, ordered_unit, est_price_cents, preference specific|best_match|refund, named_listing_id NULL). line_outcomes (order_line_id, kind found|substituted|refunded, listing_id, master_item_id, qty, weight_g NULL, amount_cents, best_match_ranking_version NULL, candidate_rank NULL, named_tried bool); invariant Σ qty = ordered_qty, checked.
  • Queries. Found rate per master item, region and week = Σ found qty ÷ Σ ordered qty over lines whose mapping at order time was that master item (state whether to use the mapping of record or the corrected mapping). Substitutes given for a master item: group substituted outcomes by ordered master item and substitute master item, with the share where the consumer named it. One order: lines with their frozen listing versions, preferences and outcomes, visible only to that consumer and support.

Competing designs to accept. A graph or document model for the catalogue with a relational order side. Storing listing versions as SCD2 rows in a lake table partitioned by date with change detection. Using the mapping current today for found rate (with a stated restatement policy) instead of the mapping at order time.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Barcode as primary key; merchant ids treated as permanent; an availability flag overwritten; the substitute written over the ordered item; outcomes that do not reconcile; weighted items counted as not found; rewriting every listing nightly at {{listings}} listings; consumer-level analytics.

Incident guidance.

  • Sizes in the name field created new master items: the matcher accepted a malformed feed. Quarantine the batch (schema and distribution checks per feed before matching), supersede the bad mappings with the previous ones, retire the spurious master items, and restate the found rates for the affected days.
  • Weighted items recorded as not found: the pick outcome conflated "found at a different weight" with "not found". Record picked weight on found outcomes, re-derive outcomes from the pick events for the affected days, and restate the region's found rate.
  • Nightly rewrite of every listing: write versions only on change (hash per listing), compact historical versions, and partition by store and validity so "as of a date" reads one partition range; at {{feed_updates}} updates a day most updates change nothing.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Close the old listing (or mapping) at the reuse date and open a new one; last month's found rate stays with the old master item. (2) Units found ÷ units ordered, per line in ordered units; for weighted items, a line is found when picked within this exercise's tolerance. (3) Parse and normalise units; match on brand, normalised size and name similarity; review below a confidence threshold. (4) Change detection, append-only versions, compaction. (5) Superseding mapping rows; reports keyed by order-time mapping can be restated for the corrected window with an audit note.

Rubric anchors. 2: one items table per store with a stock flag; substitutes overwrite the line. 3: master items, versioned listings, mapping table, signals as events, outcome rows that reconcile. 4: also mapping corrections with restatement, barcode reuse and store codes, weighted items, change-only versioning sized against volume, privacy and merchant scoping.

Strong signals. Treats the mapping as data with confidence and history; writes the reconciliation invariant. Red flags. Barcode as the key; deleting old listings; per-consumer analytics.

DSH-L3-04.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design).

  • Plans. plans (plan_id, cadence monthly|annual); plan_versions (plan_id, version, price_cents, delivery_fee_waiver bool, service_fee_discount_bps, min_subtotal_cents, valid_from, valid_to): a price change is a new version, applied at each member's next renewal.
  • Memberships and periods. memberships (membership_id, consumer_id, started_at, ended_at NULL); membership_periods (period_id, membership_id, kind trial|paid|grace|paused, plan_id, plan_version, starts_at, ends_at, created_by_event) with no overlap per membership (exclusion constraint or checks). Cancellation is an event (membership_events (membership_id, kind, at, effective_at)) that sets the end of the membership at the current period's end; it does not shorten the paid period.
  • Money. billing_attempts (attempt_id, membership_id, period_id, attempted_at, outcome, amount_cents), charges (charge_id, period_id, amount_cents, charged_at), refunds (refund_id, charge_id, amount_cents, refunded_at, reason). Annual revenue recognised per month: a derived revenue_schedule (charge_id, month, amount_cents) spreading the charge evenly (remainder cents to a stated month), reversed for unused months on refund.
  • Benefit decisions. benefit_decisions (order_id, decision_seq, is_of_record, decided_at, period_id NULL, plan_version, store_eligible, subtotal_before_promotions_cents, min_subtotal_cents, applied bool, reason, delivery_fee_waived_cents, service_fee_discount_cents). An edited order writes a new decision and marks it the one of record; reports read only is_of_record.
  • Queries. Members on date D by state: periods containing D's chosen instant (end of day in a stated zone), grouped by kind. Benefit cost per member-month: Σ waived fees of decisions of record by month ÷ member-months; revenue from the revenue schedule. "Why not O": the decision of record, its inputs and reason (below {{min_subtotal}}, store not eligible, no period in force).
  • Time. Boundaries in UTC instants; the member's local day defines trial end and renewal day; trial end = local start date + {{trial_days}} days at the local end of day, converted to UTC.

Competing designs to accept. An event-sourced membership with periods as a projection. Storing state transitions only, with periods derived by window functions. Daily membership snapshots for reporting, if the candidate shows how late refunds and corrections restate them.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. A status column with an expiry date; cancellations that cut benefits immediately; benefit decided from a recomputed subtotal later; summing every decision per order; annual revenue booked in one month; trial ends in UTC days; monthly price changes applied mid-period; analytics on individual members' order history.

Incident guidance.

  • Renewals failed during a provider outage: a failed attempt must open a grace period, not end the membership. Reopen the memberships with grace periods back-dated to the failure, refund or credit the delivery fees charged in error, retry the payments, and add an alert on the failure rate of renewals.
  • Benefit cost doubled after order edits: more than one decision was summed. Mark one decision of record per order (the last before fulfilment), restate the week from decisions of record, and add a uniqueness check on (order_id) WHERE is_of_record.
  • Trials charged a day early: the trial end used UTC days. Compute trial ends from the member's local date, refund the early charges for the affected members, and test trials started near local midnight in several zones.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Periods containing the instant, by kind; paused counted apart. (2) The current monthly period ends now (or at its end, per this exercise's rule); a new annual period starts; the unused part of the month is credited against the annual charge with a recorded proration. (3) The existing member's next period uses the new plan version; revenue changes from that month. (4) The decision of record with its inputs and reason. (5) Monthly aggregates from decisions of record and the revenue schedule; a late refund restates the revenue schedule rows for unused months only.

Rubric anchors. 2: a member table with status and expiry; benefits inferred later from fees. 3: plans with versions, periods with states, charges and refunds, a benefit decision per order with inputs. 4: also one decision of record with edits, revenue spread across months, local-time trials and renewals, grace handling, and incidents repaired by correcting periods and decisions.

Strong signals. Separates relationship, periods and money; makes benefit decisions reproducible. Red flags. Recomputing past benefits from today's rules; cutting benefits at cancellation time; floating-point money.

DSH-L3-05.html:
Reference solution (PostgreSQL)

WITH days AS (
  SELECT s.store_id, d::date AS on_date
  FROM stores s
  CROSS JOIN generate_series(DATE '{{first_day}}' - 1, DATE '{{last_day}}', INTERVAL '1 day') AS d
), listed AS (
  SELECT dy.store_id, dy.on_date, h.open_time, h.close_time
  FROM days dy
  JOIN holiday_hours h ON h.store_id = dy.store_id AND h.holiday_date = dy.on_date
  WHERE h.open_time IS NOT NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT dy.store_id, dy.on_date, w.open_time, w.close_time
  FROM days dy
  JOIN weekly_hours w ON w.store_id = dy.store_id AND w.iso_weekday = EXTRACT(ISODOW FROM dy.on_date)
  WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM holiday_hours h
                    WHERE h.store_id = dy.store_id AND h.holiday_date = dy.on_date)
), open_iv AS (
  SELECT store_id,
         on_date + open_time AS opens_at,
         CASE WHEN close_time > open_time THEN on_date + close_time
              ELSE (on_date + 1) + close_time END AS closes_at
  FROM listed
), pz AS (
  SELECT store_id, paused_at,
         COALESCE(resumed_at, TIMESTAMP '{{sample_end}}') AS resumed_at
  FROM pauses
), weeks AS (
  SELECT s.store_id, w::date AS week_start
  FROM stores s
  CROSS JOIN generate_series(DATE '{{first_day}}', DATE '{{last_day}}', INTERVAL '7 days') AS w
), flagged AS (
  SELECT o.store_id,
         date_trunc('week', o.accepted_at)::date AS week_start,
         EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pz p
                 WHERE p.store_id = o.store_id
                   AND p.paused_at <= o.accepted_at AND o.accepted_at < p.resumed_at) AS paused,
         NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM open_iv v
                     WHERE v.store_id = o.store_id
                       AND v.opens_at <= o.accepted_at AND o.accepted_at < v.closes_at) AS outside
  FROM orders o
), order_counts AS (
  SELECT store_id, week_start,
         COUNT(*) AS orders_accepted,
         COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE paused OR outside) AS orders_while_closed,
         COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE paused) AS orders_while_paused
  FROM flagged
  GROUP BY store_id, week_start
), pieces AS (
  SELECT wk.store_id, wk.week_start,
         GREATEST(p.paused_at, v.opens_at, wk.week_start::timestamp) AS piece_start,
         LEAST(p.resumed_at, v.closes_at, wk.week_start::timestamp + INTERVAL '7 days') AS piece_end
  FROM weeks wk
  JOIN pz p ON p.store_id = wk.store_id
  JOIN open_iv v ON v.store_id = wk.store_id
), paused_minutes AS (
  SELECT store_id, week_start,
         SUM(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM piece_end - piece_start)) / 60 AS minutes_paused
  FROM pieces
  WHERE piece_end > piece_start
  GROUP BY store_id, week_start
)
SELECT wk.store_id,
       wk.week_start,
       COALESCE(c.orders_accepted, 0) AS orders_accepted,
       COALESCE(c.orders_while_closed, 0) AS orders_while_closed,
       COALESCE(c.orders_while_paused, 0) AS orders_while_paused,
       COALESCE(m.minutes_paused, 0)::int AS minutes_paused
FROM weeks wk
LEFT JOIN order_counts c ON c.store_id = wk.store_id AND c.week_start = wk.week_start
LEFT JOIN paused_minutes m ON m.store_id = wk.store_id AND m.week_start = wk.week_start
ORDER BY wk.store_id, wk.week_start;

Explanation. The query first turns the hours into real intervals: one row per store and date from the day before the sample through the last day, joined to the date's holiday rows when there are any (NULL rows mean closed, so they produce no interval) and otherwise to the weekly rows for that ISO weekday. date + time gives a timestamp, and when close_time is earlier than open_time the close moves to the next date, so an interval stays with the date it opened on and still covers the early hours of a holiday or of the first day. Pauses get an end of {{sample_end}} when resumed_at is NULL. Each order is then flagged with two half-open tests, and one COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE paused OR outside) counts an order that is both only once. Paused minutes are the positive pieces of a three-way intersection (pause ∩ listed interval ∩ week); because a store's intervals and pauses never overlap among themselves, the pieces never overlap and their sum is exact. The final select starts from every store crossed with every week, so store-weeks with no orders keep a row.

Complexity. Intervals: stores × (days + 1) × intervals per day. Order flags are two correlated lookups per order, served by indexes on (store_id, opens_at) and (store_id, paused_at). The minutes join is pauses × intervals × weeks per store, filtered to positive pieces; in production a range join (tsrange && with a GiST index) or a pre-built per-store interval table keeps it near linear. At hundreds of thousands of stores, the derived intervals are materialised (DSH-L3-02) rather than generated per run.

Dialect notes. generate_series over dates, date + time, date + integer, EXTRACT(ISODOW …) and FILTER (WHERE …) are PostgreSQL. BigQuery: UNNEST(GENERATE_DATE_ARRAY(…)), DATETIME(date, time), EXTRACT(DAYOFWEEK …) (1 = Sunday, so remap), COUNTIF, DATETIME_DIFF(…, MINUTE), DATE_TRUNC(d, WEEK(MONDAY)). Snowflake: a row generator or calendar table, TIMESTAMP_NTZ_FROM_PARTS(date, time), DAYOFWEEKISO, COUNT_IF, DATEDIFF('minute', …); DATE_TRUNC('week', …) follows the WEEK_START parameter. Spark SQL: explode(sequence(…)), make_timestamp or string concatenation, dayofweek (1 = Sunday), count_if. MySQL 8: a recursive CTE or calendar table, TIMESTAMP(date, time), WEEKDAY() (0 = Monday), SUM(CASE …), TIMESTAMPDIFF(MINUTE, …). PostgreSQL's GREATEST/LEAST ignore NULL arguments, while in MySQL, Snowflake and BigQuery a single NULL argument makes the result NULL; replacing a NULL resumed_at first keeps the query portable. None of these variants is executed here.

Edge cases built into the data. Orders exactly at an open_time (open) and exactly at a close_time (closed); orders exactly at paused_at (paused) and exactly at resumed_at (not paused); a pause that runs past closing with an order inside it after closing (paused and outside, counted once) and paused minutes counted only up to closing; a holiday closed all day with an order at a time the weekly hours would have been open; a holiday with short hours; a weekday with no rows; one store-week with no orders. Hard adds split lunch and dinner hours with an order between them, a late-night store whose hours cross midnight, an order in the first minutes of the sample served by the previous evening's interval, a pause across the Sunday–Monday week boundary, and a pause that starts before opening. Very Hard adds the late store closed for a holiday while the previous evening's hours still run into it (with an order there), holiday hours that themselves cross midnight, a pause that began before the sample, and a pause with no resumed_at at the end of the sample.

Common mistakes. Starting from orders (store-weeks with no orders vanish); BETWEEN or <= at close_time or resumed_at; adding holiday hours to the weekly hours instead of replacing them; cutting intervals at midnight; generating dates from first_day instead of the day before; applying a holiday to the previous night's late shift; counting paused minutes outside listed hours; giving a pause's minutes to the week it started in; summing paused and outside flags; dropping pauses with NULL resumed_at (or ending them at now(), which makes a historical report change on every rerun). Each of these except now() has a diagnostic.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Store an IANA time zone per store, keep hours as local wall-clock times, convert each derived interval to timestamptz with AT TIME ZONE; minutes are elapsed minutes between instants, so the fall-back night's late shift is an hour longer (state that rule). (2) Overlapping pauses double count minutes and orders stay correct (EXISTS); merge pauses per store first (gaps-and-islands with a running max of ends) or compute minutes against the union. (3) Assign one cause by a stated precedence (paused, then holiday closure, then outside weekly hours) and report the overlap separately if needed. (4) Materialise per-store open intervals as tsrange rows for a rolling horizon, invalidated by hours edits, holiday entries and time zone changes; pauses are already intervals; the weekly report then joins three range tables.

Rubric anchors. 2: hours compared as times of day only (no dates), midnight crossing or holidays ignored, rows only for store-weeks with orders. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also explains time zones and daylight saving, overlapping pauses, cause attribution and materialisation of intervals.

Strong signals. Builds intervals per date before touching orders; asks about midnight and the day before the sample; states half-open boundaries. Red flags. Comparing accepted_at::time BETWEEN open_time AND close_time; now() in a historical report; counting an order twice.

Incident guidance.

  • A third of a late store's orders outside hours: intervals were cut at midnight. Fix the close to move to the next date, rerun the affected weeks, and add a test with an order at 00:30 for a store open past midnight.
  • Previous night's late orders flagged on a holiday: holiday rows were applied by calendar time rather than by the date an interval opens. Apply overrides only to intervals that open on the holiday date, rerun, and tell the affected merchants that the earlier numbers were wrong.
  • Thousands of paused minutes from open pauses: automatic pauses never ended. Keep counting to the end of the period (the rule), but flag pauses open longer than a threshold, close the stuck ones at the device's reconnection time, and restate the weeks once corrected.
